content: I'm a complete novice at this. Why does a lens make a picture larger or smaller? I believe a wider lens always gives more magnification, because it collects light across a bigger area. Is that basically how image size is decided?

A wider lens can collect more light, but it does not by itself set the magnification. Image size mainly depends on the lens's focal length and the distances between the object, lens, and image. The lens redirects light from each point of the object so those rays meet again. Where they meet determines the image position; the geometry of those paths determines its size.

What does it mean for light from one point to meet again? Light seems to leave the whole object in every direction, so I do not see how the lens keeps the top and bottom parts from getting mixed together.

Each tiny point on the object sends rays in many directions. The lens bends the rays from one object point so they converge at one corresponding image point. Rays from the object's top converge somewhere different from rays from its bottom. They cross without affecting one another, much like two flashlight beams can overlap while still continuing along their own paths.
Then why can I move a screen back and forth and find only one sharp place? I assumed the picture existed all along the light path and the screen merely caught a different-sized slice of it.

Away from the image plane, rays from each object point have not yet met, or have already met and spread apart again. A screen there receives a small patch rather than a sharp point, so neighboring patches overlap and blur. At the image plane, each bundle narrows to its matching point. The screen does not create that geometry; it makes the focused light pattern visible.
So if I keep the same lens and object position but cover the outer half of the glass, should the picture stay the same size and just become dimmer? What would make it blur instead?

Yes. Covering part of an ideal lens removes some rays from every image point, so the whole image remains and keeps the same size, but becomes dimmer. It may also lose some fine detail because the usable opening is smaller. Ordinary blur comes from placing the screen away from the image plane, imperfect lens shapes, or different colors focusing at slightly different distances.

I'm new to optics. What is focal length when a lens is actually making an image? I think it changes as I move the object closer, since the sharp picture shifts and the lens seems to be focusing at a new distance.

Focal length is a property of the lens and its surrounding material, not the object's position. For a simple converging lens, it is the distance at which nearly parallel incoming rays come together. Moving the object changes the image distance because the incoming rays now reach the lens at different angles. The focusing situation changes, but the lens's focal length stays essentially constant.
Why do parallel rays get a special distance? Light from a nearby lamp is spreading out, not arriving in parallel lines, so I am unclear about how that fixed distance helps predict the lamp's picture.

Parallel rays are a convenient reference case: they represent light from an object extremely far away. The fixed focal length tells us the lens's bending strength. For a nearby lamp, the rays arrive while spreading, so the lens must spend some of its bending merely making them parallel before bringing them together. Consequently, their image forms farther from the lens than the focal point.
If I slide the lamp toward the lens, does the sharp picture always move farther away? I can picture that trend, but I do not know whether it continues right up until the lamp touches the glass.

It moves farther away only while the lamp remains beyond one focal length. As the lamp approaches that boundary, the image distance grows very large. At exactly one focal length, the outgoing rays are parallel, so no finite screen position catches a sharp image. Move the lamp closer still, and the rays leave while spreading; the lens then produces a virtual image instead.
What is a virtual image in ordinary terms? Does that mean there is no picture at all, or that the picture is somewhere a screen cannot reach even though an eye can still see it?

The second description is closer. The outgoing rays do not physically meet, so a screen cannot intercept a focused pattern. However, your eye traces those spreading rays backward in straight lines. They appear to come from a common point on the object's side of the lens, producing a visible virtual image. A magnifying glass used close to an object works this way.

Then when I move the lamp, I am changing where the image forms, not changing the lens's own focal length. Is the simple rule that objects beyond that fixed length can make screen pictures, while closer objects cannot?

For a single converging lens and a real object, that is the useful rule. Beyond one focal length, the lens forms a real, inverted image that a screen can catch. Inside one focal length, it forms an upright, magnified virtual image. Exactly at the focal distance is the limiting case, with outgoing rays parallel and the image effectively at infinity.

I'm a total beginner with lenses. Why does a magnifying glass show an upright enlarged object, while the same piece of glass can project an upside-down picture onto paper? I thought its size alone fixed how strongly it magnified.

The difference comes from object distance, not simply the glass's diameter. Hold the object closer than the lens's focal length and the outgoing rays spread in a way your eye interprets as a larger, upright virtual image. Put the object beyond the focal length and the rays actually converge on the far side, creating a real image that is inverted and can land on paper.

What makes the projected picture turn upside down? I imagine the lens flipping the light inside the glass, almost like rotating a little copy, but that seems vague when every part is sending light everywhere.

The lens does not rotate a stored copy. Consider rays leaving the top of the object: after refraction, a useful bundle converges below the central line on the far side. Rays from the bottom converge above it. The bundles cross as they travel, so the arrangement of image points is inverted. Each image point is constructed independently from rays coming from its matching object point.

Why does looking through the glass avoid that crossing? Is my eye placed before the rays have had enough room to cross, or are the rays following a completely different pattern when the object is close?

They follow a different pattern because the close object sends strongly diverging rays into the lens. The lens bends them inward, but not enough to make them meet after the glass. Your eye receives rays that are still spreading and traces them backward to an upright virtual image. It is not merely catching the same real image before a later crossing; no real crossing occurs there.

Suppose I use a dinner-plate-sized lens with the same curve as a small magnifying glass. Would the larger one mainly look brighter rather than make the letters larger, assuming I hold both at the same distances?

Broadly, yes. If both lenses have the same material, surface curvature, and therefore focal length, using them at the same object and viewing distances gives similar magnification. The wider lens admits rays through a larger opening, which can increase brightness and alter the visible field. In practice, its outer regions may also introduce more distortion or colored fringes unless the lens is well corrected.

What actually sets the focal length if width does not? Is it mostly how bulged the surfaces are, or does the kind of glass matter enough that two equally shaped lenses could form pictures at different places?

Both curvature and material matter. More strongly curved surfaces usually bend rays more and give a shorter focal length. A material with a higher refractive index also bends light more at the same surface shape, again shortening the focal length. The material surrounding the lens matters too, which is why a lens can behave differently in air and when submerged in water.
If the projected image is upside down, can I make it upright merely by moving the paper, or would I need another lens or mirror to turn the ray pattern over a second time?

Moving the paper changes focus and image size, but it does not reverse the orientation while you stay on the same real-image branch. To obtain an upright projected image, you generally need another optical step, such as a second lens that forms another image, or mirrors arranged to change orientation. Simply rotating the paper would rotate the surface, not reconstruct the light pattern upright.

I'm a complete novice at image formation. What is the lens doing when a camera focuses on a face and then on a distant building? I believe moving the subject changes the lens's focal length, because the focus setting clearly changes.

In a simple camera, changing subject distance changes the required distance between the lens and sensor, while the lens's focal length remains fixed. Light from the distant building arrives almost parallel and forms an image near the focal plane. Light from the nearer face arrives more spread out and forms its sharp image slightly farther behind the lens, so the camera shifts optical parts to match.
Why does the face become fuzzy when the sensor stays in the building position? Are the face rays missing the sensor, or do they reach it but land in the wrong places around each intended point?

They reach the sensor, but each object point produces a small blurred patch instead of a point. At the building-focused sensor position, rays from a point on the nearer face are still converging and have not reached their narrowest bundle. Those patches overlap with patches from neighboring facial points, erasing fine boundaries. The total light can still arrive even though its spatial arrangement is unfocused.
What does closing the camera's little opening change? I have seen that a smaller opening can make more distances look sharp, but it seems as though less light should only make the same blur darker.

A smaller opening does reduce light, but it also admits a narrower cone of rays from each object point. When the sensor is slightly away from that point's ideal image plane, the narrower cone makes a smaller blur patch. That increases the range of distances that look acceptably sharp. The tradeoffs are a dimmer image and, at very small openings, softening from diffraction.
Is that why a pinhole can make a picture without any lens? If only a narrow bundle gets through, I assume rays from different parts of the scene are kept from spreading across the whole screen.

Exactly. A tiny hole selects a narrow set of paths from each scene point. Light from the top of an object reaches a lower part of the screen, while light from the bottom reaches higher up, producing an inverted image. No refraction is needed. A larger hole brightens the picture but lets each scene point paint a wider patch, so the image blurs.
Then why bother with a lens instead of using a very tiny hole? Does the lens mainly gather many more rays while still steering those from each scene point toward the matching place on the sensor?

Yes. A lens accepts a much wider bundle from each scene point and redirects that bundle toward one image point, giving a far brighter image than a pinhole can provide at comparable sharpness. It also allows deliberate control of focus and image scale. The price is added complexity: real lenses can distort, separate colors, and focus imperfectly away from their chosen plane.

When a phone says it has optical zoom, is it moving lenses to change their combined focal length rather than changing focal length just because the person moved? I want to separate those two kinds of change.

That is the right distinction. Moving the subject changes object distance and therefore where a given lens system forms its image; it does not by itself change the system's focal length. Optical zoom deliberately rearranges lens groups so the whole system has a different effective focal length and image scale. Some phones instead switch between fixed lens modules or crop digitally, which is not continuous optical zoom.
If I focus closer by moving the lens away from the sensor, will the face also become slightly larger on the sensor? Or is focus position separate from the size of the formed image?

The face generally becomes larger as you focus closer with a simple lens, because image distance increases while object distance decreases. Magnification is tied to the ratio of those distances, so focus position and image size are geometrically connected. In compound camera lenses, internal focusing can modify that trend, sometimes noticeably, because different groups move and the effective focal length may change slightly during focusing.
